correctness.rationale: The theorem is conditional on an objective true label, independent categorical responses with each correct-label probability at least both incorrect-label probabilities, uniform subsets, and fair plurality tie-breaking. For every one of 81 deterministic 4-vote profiles the four-minus-average-three influence is zero except patterns 2-1-1, where it equals 1/3 (true doubled) or -1/6 (false doubled). The probability difference is (2P0-P1-P2)/6. Every admissible three-coordinate probability row is an explicit convex mixture of four listed rational vertices; the gain is separately affine in four rows. The 4^4=256 vertex assignments reduce by permutation to 35 exact rational types. Exact independent evaluations both by vote-profile averaging and by the 2-1-1 event identity give minimum 0 and maximum 1/12; the witness (perfect,perfect,binary-0/1,binary-0/2) gives four accuracy 1 and random-three accuracy 11/12. For any N>=4, sampling a uniform four-person set and deleting a uniform member produces a uniform three-person set by (N-3)/(4*C(N,4))=1/C(N,3), so the result averages exact four-person bounds. Computations independently reproduced from package VERIFY.py and a complete 35-entry rational table included in RESULT.md. No floating inference, timeout, or unproved infinite assertion is used.

originality.rationale: Binary Berend--Sapir (2005) Theorem 1 implies a *zero* three-to-four increment only in dichotomous majority, so cannot imply the strictly positive three-label example; its abstract, definitions, main theorem, proof and discussion were inspected in the author-provided full text. Goertz--Maniquet (2011) treats three-alternative plurality but examines large strategic Poisson elections and information-efficient Nash equilibria; its full 19-page working paper model, theorems, argument, and conclusion were compared with finite independent fixed-label panel accuracy and do not entail a bound of 1/12. Saari (2002) develops three-alternative voting-profile decompositions without a finite conditional independently correct jury framework in its available abstract; its full text could not be inspected, retained as a specific residual risk. Indexed scientific-literature searches for the 2-1-1 identity, committee sizes, alias formulations and precise constant returned no covering theorem. Originality is assessed relative to these actual comparisons rather than inferred solely from failed search; broader unknown coverage is possible.
residual_risks: Saari (2002) original full paper could not be materially inspected; plausible but abstract indicates distinct deterministic positional-profile scope.
A more general multi-alternative independently correct jury theorem or a specialized multinomial reliability inequality absent from sampled databases might imply the 1/12 bound.
No independent scholarly or external audit was performed.

value.rationale: The four-versus-three comparison is the first odd-to-even committee-size comparison at which binary fair majority gives identically zero marginal information, making three-label plurality its natural minimal extension. The new exact interval [0,1/12] and attaining heterogeneous panel quantify the sharp possible gain and guarantee there is no loss for all finite electorates, independent of panel size and heterogeneous individual modal accuracies. A 1/12 gain is an appreciable 8.33 percentage points and the exact bound is a directly usable benchmark for annotator panels and ternary fact-finding juries. Neither code reproducibility nor mere novelty is used as a substitute for this structural application. No claims about strategic utility or correlated voters are made.
